title: Phase Change
description: Phase changes occur when matter changes state. Heating adds energy causing melting and evaporation. Cooling removes energy causing condensation and freezing.

exercises.question: What is a PHASE CHANGE?
choices: a chemical change creating a new substance
when matter changes from one state to another
exercises.exp: A phase change is when matter changes state — solid to liquid, liquid to gas, etc. No new substance is created!

exercises.question: Which phase change needs ENERGY to be ADDED?
exercises.exp: Melting needs heat energy added to break apart the tightly-packed solid particles.

exercises.question: Which phase change releases ENERGY to the surroundings?
exercises.exp: Freezing releases energy — water loses heat to its surroundings as it turns into ice.

exercises.question: Water boils at 100°C. What phase change occurs at boiling point?
exercises.exp: At 100°C, liquid water turns to water vapour (gas) — this is evaporation / boiling.

exercises.question: Water freezes at 0°C. What phase change occurs at 0°C?
exercises.exp: At 0°C, liquid water loses heat and becomes solid ice — this is freezing.

exercises.question: Dew on grass in the morning is formed by ___.
choices: water vapour in the air condensing onto cool surfaces overnight
exercises.exp: At night, surfaces cool and water vapour in the air condenses into liquid droplets — morning dew!

exercises.question: When sweat evaporates from your skin, your skin feels ___.
choices: colder — evaporation takes heat energy away from your skin
exercises.exp: Evaporation takes energy from your skin to turn liquid into gas — that is why sweating cools you down!

exercises.question: During a phase change, the TEMPERATURE of the substance ___.
choices: stays constant until the entire phase change is complete
exercises.exp: During a phase change, all added energy goes into changing state — temperature stays flat until the change is complete.

exercises.question: The reverse of CONDENSATION is ___.
exercises.exp: Condensation = gas → liquid. Evaporation = liquid → gas. They are opposites!

exercises.question: Dry ice (solid CO₂) changes directly from SOLID to GAS without becoming a liquid. This is called ___.
exercises.exp: Sublimation is when a solid turns directly into a gas, skipping the liquid phase. Dry ice does this!

exercises.question: Ice in a freezer at -10°C is heated slowly. At what temperature will it start to MELT?
exercises.exp: Ice always melts at 0°C (at normal pressure). It stays at 0°C while melting, then warms once all ice is gone.

exercises.question: Which change-of-state diagram is CORRECT?
exercises.exp: Melting goes from solid to liquid (adding heat). Freezing goes from liquid to solid (removing heat).

exercises.question: What is DEPOSITION (the opposite of sublimation)?
choices: gas turning directly into solid without becoming liquid first
exercises.exp: Deposition is when gas turns directly into solid — the reverse of sublimation! Frost on windows forms by deposition of water vapour.

exercises.question: You heat an ice cube. First it melts at 0°C, then the water heats up. When does it START to boil?
choices: as soon as all the ice is gone
as soon as you add heat
exercises.exp: Liquid water heats from 0°C toward 100°C. Boiling (evaporation throughout the liquid) begins at exactly 100°C at sea level.

exercises.question: A puddle DISAPPEARS on a warm sunny day even though the temperature is below 100°C. How?
choices: slow evaporation — water molecules at the surface have enough energy to escape into the air even below 100°C
exercises.exp: Evaporation can happen at any temperature — some surface molecules always have enough energy to escape into the air. Sun speeds it up!

exercises.question: On a HOT humid day, you notice water droplets forming on a cold glass of lemonade. This is ___.
choices: condensation — warm moist air touches the cold glass and water vapour becomes liquid
the glass sweating its own water
exercises.exp: Cold glass cools nearby air below its dew point — water vapour condenses on the glass surface. The glass is not leaking!

exercises.question: During MELTING, energy is added but temperature stays at 0°C. Where does the energy go?
choices: it breaks bonds between solid particles to change their arrangement — not raise temperature
it heats the air around the ice
exercises.exp: The added energy breaks the strong bonds holding solid particles in fixed positions — this phase change energy is called latent heat.

exercises.question: What is the MELTING POINT of a substance?
choices: the temperature at which it becomes a gas
the exact temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid
the temperature at which it condenses
the temperature at which it sublimes
exercises.exp: The melting point is specific to each substance — water melts at 0°C, iron at 1538°C. It is also the freezing point (same temperature, opposite direction)!

exercises.question: What is the BOILING POINT of water at sea level?
exercises.exp: Water boils at 100°C at sea level (where air pressure is standard). At high altitudes, air pressure is lower and water boils below 100°C!

exercises.question: A chef boils water to cook pasta. She turns DOWN the heat once it is boiling. The water KEEPS boiling. Why?
choices: boiling water always needs maximum heat
once boiling, 100°C is maintained — you only need enough heat to maintain the phase change, not more
lower heat makes water boil more
exercises.exp: Boiling water stays at 100°C — adding more heat just makes more steam, not hotter water. Lower heat is enough to maintain boiling.

exercises.question: Moth balls (naphthalene) are solid and slowly release a strong smell without becoming liquid. This is ___.
exercises.exp: Naphthalene sublimes at room temperature — it goes directly from solid to gas, which is why you smell it without seeing liquid!

exercises.question: EVAPORATION happens at the surface of a liquid. BOILING happens throughout the liquid. What do they have in common?
choices: both are liquid → gas phase changes
exercises.exp: Both evaporation and boiling change liquid into gas — evaporation is slow and at the surface; boiling is fast and throughout.

exercises.question: A scientist heats wax. It melts at 65°C and boils at 340°C. At 100°C, what state is the wax?
exercises.exp: 100°C is above the melting point (65°C) but below the boiling point (340°C) — so wax is liquid at 100°C.

exercises.question: Why does SWEATING cool your body down?
choices: sweat is very cold when it leaves the skin
evaporation of sweat absorbs heat energy from your skin to change state
sweating speeds up blood flow only
exercises.exp: Evaporation requires energy — it takes that energy from your skin as heat, cooling your body temperature. Sweating is your body's AC!

exercises.question: A substance can be MELTED and REFROZEN multiple times. What does this tell us?
choices: it is a physical (reversible) change — the substance is unchanged chemically
the substance is destroyed each time
exercises.exp: Phase changes are physical changes — the substance is chemically the same after melting and refreezing. No new substance is created.

exercises.question: What is FREEZING POINT?
choices: the temperature at which a gas becomes a liquid
the temperature at which a liquid changes to a solid
the temperature at which a solid sublimates
exercises.exp: The freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid turns to solid. For water it is 0°C, but every substance has its own freezing point.

exercises.question: When liquid water FREEZES in a crack in a rock and expands, the rock can SPLIT. Why does ice expand?
choices: water gets heavier when it freezes
water molecules form a crystal lattice that takes up more space than liquid water
ice is lighter so it floats and pushes
the cold makes rock weaker only
exercises.exp: Water is unusual — when it freezes, its molecules form a hexagonal lattice that actually takes up MORE space than liquid water. This expansion splits rock!

exercises.question: Why does HIGH ALTITUDE (like mountaintops) cause water to boil BELOW 100°C?
choices: mountaintops are closer to the sun
lower air pressure at altitude means less force pressing on the water surface, so molecules escape (boil) more easily at lower temperatures
exercises.exp: Boiling point depends on air pressure. Less air pressure = easier escape for molecules = lower boiling point. Water boils at ~70°C on Mount Everest!

exercises.question: A glass of water is left uncovered for one week. What will happen to its volume?
choices: it will stay exactly the same
it will decrease — water evaporates over time
exercises.exp: Slow evaporation removes water molecules from the surface continuously — the glass level drops over time even at room temperature.

exercises.question: What is the correct word for gas → liquid phase change?
exercises.exp: Condensation = gas → liquid. Think of water droplets forming on a cold window or mirror — that is condensation!

exercises.question: Dry ice is solid CO₂ at -78°C. If you bring it into a warm room, it releases a fog-like vapour. What is happening?
choices: it is melting into liquid CO₂ then evaporating
it is subliming — going directly from solid to gas, and the cold gas condenses water vapour in the air, making fog
it is condensing water from the air
exercises.exp: Dry ice sublimes (solid→gas directly). The extremely cold CO₂ gas condenses water vapour in the surrounding air into tiny droplets — fog!

exercises.question: During CONDENSATION, the gas loses energy. Where does that energy go?
choices: it is released into the surroundings as heat
it goes back into the gas
exercises.exp: Phase changes release or absorb energy. Condensation releases heat energy into surroundings — that is why humid air feels warmer when it releases rain!

exercises.question: Phase changes are PHYSICAL changes. Which statement supports this?
choices: phase changes create entirely new substances
the chemical composition stays the same — H₂O is always H₂O whether solid, liquid, or gas
exercises.exp: Ice, water, and steam are all H₂O — same chemical formula, different arrangement. No new substance is created. Physical change!

exercises.question: LATENT HEAT is the energy needed to change state WITHOUT changing temperature. During a phase change, temperature ___.
choices: stays constant while energy is used to change the state instead
exercises.exp: Latent heat: energy goes into breaking/forming particle bonds, not warming the substance. Ice melting stays at 0°C until all ice is liquid!

exercises.question: What is the FREEZING POINT of water?
exercises.exp: Water freezes at 0°C. The freezing point and melting point are the SAME temperature — 0°C — just approached from different directions.

exercises.question: Salt lowers the freezing point of water below 0°C. Why is SALT spread on icy roads in winter?
choices: salt colours the road for visibility
salt water freezes at a lower temperature, so it melts ice on the road
exercises.exp: Adding salt to water lowers its freezing point (freezing point depression). Salt on roads makes ice melt even when the temperature is below 0°C!

exercises.question: Sweat evaporating from your skin makes you feel COOL because ___.
choices: evaporation releases heat into your skin
evaporation ABSORBS heat energy from your skin to change state — taking heat away
cold air replaces warm air on your skin
exercises.exp: Evaporation is endothermic — it absorbs heat. Sweat evaporating removes heat energy FROM your skin, cooling you down. Brilliant body cooling system!

exercises.question: Which phase change RELEASES energy to the surroundings?
choices: freezing — liquid releases energy as it solidifies
exercises.exp: Freezing, condensation, and deposition ALL release energy. When water freezes, it releases latent heat — this is why frost nights are often slightly less cold than expected!

exercises.question: When water boils at 100°C, the temperature does NOT rise above 100°C as long as water remains. Why?
choices: it is impossible to add more heat at boiling point
all added heat energy goes into breaking particle bonds (latent heat of vaporisation), not raising temperature
water absorbs light at 100°C instead of heat
exercises.exp: At boiling point, all added energy breaks intermolecular bonds — liquid → gas. Temperature stays at 100°C until ALL water has evaporated!

exercises.question: A phase change diagram shows PLATEAUS at 0°C and 100°C for water. These plateaus represent ___.
choices: times when no energy is being added
the phase changes of melting (0°C) and boiling (100°C) where temperature stays constant during state change
the freezing and condensing points only
exercises.exp: On a heating curve, flat plateaus show phase changes. Energy is being added the whole time but goes into changing state, not raising temperature.

exercises.question: Why does a WET TOWEL on your head help reduce a fever?
choices: the cold towel conducts heat into your head
evaporation of water from the towel absorbs heat energy from your skin, lowering its temperature
the weight of the towel reduces blood pressure
exercises.exp: Water evaporating from the towel is an endothermic process — it absorbs heat from your head to evaporate, reducing your fever!

exercises.question: Which state change is ENDOTHERMIC (absorbs heat from surroundings)?
choices: evaporation — it absorbs energy to turn liquid into gas
exercises.exp: Endothermic = heat absorbed. Melting, evaporation, sublimation all absorb heat. Exothermic = heat released: freezing, condensation, deposition release heat.

exercises.question: In the WATER CYCLE, which two phase changes happen in the atmosphere?
choices: evaporation (liquid → gas) and condensation (gas → liquid water droplets in clouds)
exercises.exp: Water evaporates from oceans/lakes (liquid→gas). In cool upper atmosphere, it condenses (gas→liquid) forming cloud droplets — two key water cycle phase changes!

exercises.question: Why is the TRIPLE POINT of water special?
choices: it is where water is most dense
it is where water has maximum pressure
it is the exact temperature and pressure where all three states (solid, liquid, gas) can exist simultaneously
it is the temperature at which water boils fastest
exercises.exp: The triple point (0.01°C, 611.7 Pa) is unique — all three phases of water coexist in perfect equilibrium. It is used to calibrate thermometers precisely!

exercises.question: PRESSURE affects the boiling point of water. At HIGH altitude (low pressure), water boils ___.
choices: at a lower temperature than 100°C — making it harder to cook food
at a higher temperature and faster
exercises.exp: Lower air pressure means water molecules escape to gas phase more easily at lower temperatures. On Mount Everest, water boils at about 70°C — food cooks more slowly!

exercises.question: Why does a PRESSURE COOKER cook food FASTER?
choices: increased pressure raises the boiling point of water above 100°C — food cooks at higher temperature
it uses electricity instead of gas
it reduces the amount of water needed
exercises.exp: Higher pressure raises water's boiling point (to ~120°C). Hotter water cooks food faster — a pressure cooker can cook beans in 10 minutes instead of an hour!

exercises.question: REGELATION is the phenomenon where ice melts under pressure and refreezes when pressure is removed. This explains how ___.
choices: ice cream freezes in a freezer
a glacier moves — the base melts under enormous pressure, allowing the glacier to slide
exercises.exp: Regelation: the enormous pressure at the base of a glacier slightly lowers the melting point — the bottom melts, the glacier slides on a thin water film, then refreezes!

exercises.question: What do the words ENDOTHERMIC and EXOTHERMIC literally mean?
exercises.exp: Endo = inside (heat goes IN/absorbed). Exo = outside (heat comes OUT/released). Endothermic absorbs; exothermic releases. Melting is endo; freezing is exo!

exercises.question: Clouds form at HIGH ALTITUDE. What phase change creates them?
choices: freezing — water freezes at high altitude
condensation — water vapour cools and condenses into tiny liquid droplets
exercises.exp: As moist air rises and cools, water vapour reaches its dew point and condenses into millions of tiny liquid droplets — forming clouds!

exercises.question: Why does a LAKE take longer to freeze than a shallow puddle?
choices: lakes have salt which prevents freezing
a lake contains much more water — more energy must be removed to freeze it all — latent heat of freezing for more water takes longer
puddles freeze from the bottom up
exercises.exp: Larger mass of water requires more energy removal. Each kilogram of water releases 334,000 J during freezing (latent heat) — lakes have millions of kg to freeze!

exercises.question: During FREEZE-DRYING (used for instant coffee and astronaut food), food is first frozen then water is removed by ___.
choices: sublimation — frozen water turns directly to vapour under low pressure, skipping the liquid stage
exercises.exp: Freeze-drying uses sublimation under low pressure — frozen water vapourises directly without becoming liquid, leaving dry food that rehydrates easily and stores for years!
